rich_summary: Krishna explains the doctrine of the three gunas—Goodness (sattva), Passion (rajas), and Darkness (tamas)—which bind the embodied soul to worldly existence. Goodness illuminates and produces knowledge and happiness; Passion arises from desire and drives restless action; Darkness springs from ignorance and leads to delusion, inertia, and error. A person’s dominant quality shapes their behavior, destiny, and rebirth. The wise recognize that these qualities alone act, and by detaching from them they transcend birth and suffering. Krishna then describes the person beyond the gunas: equanimous, impartial to praise or blame, pleasure or pain. The chapter continues with the cosmic Asvattha tree metaphor of worldly existence and culminates in Krishna revealing himself as Purushottama, the Supreme Being sustaining all life and the ultimate object of knowledge.

highlight_spans.why: Introduces the three qualities and how Goodness binds the soul through happiness and knowledge.
A pivotal summary of how Goodness, Passion, and Darkness connect the soul respectively to pleasure, action, and ignorance.
Explains the destinies associated with each guna and how they shape rebirth and spiritual progress.
Krishna defines the traits of one who has transcended the gunas—equanimity toward pleasure, pain, praise, blame, and all dualities.
The symbolic description of the inverted Asvattha tree representing the structure of worldly existence and attachment.
Krishna’s declaration as Purushottama, the Supreme Being beyond both the mutable and immutable—an emotional and theological climax.

top_scenes.scene_text: A vast cosmic Asvattha tree with roots glowing in the heavens and branches spreading downward across worlds while a seeker cuts it with a radiant sword of detachment.
Three luminous forces—golden light (Goodness), fiery red energy (Passion), and dark mist (Darkness)—twisting around a human figure representing the soul.
Krishna revealed as the supreme cosmic presence, radiating light that becomes the sun, moon, and fire while all beings rest within his presence.
